claims.statement: MOTS-c was nominated for FDA's 503A Bulk Drug Substances list but the nomination was withdrawn; FDA's own note on the withdrawn-nominations table states it identified no human exposure data for MOTS-c via any route of administration and lacks information on whether MOTS-c would cause harm if administered to humans, while also flagging potential immunogenicity risk from peptide-related impurities.

FDA has not identified any human exposure data on drug products containing MOTs-C administered via any route of administration. FDA lacks important information regarding any safety issues raised by MOTs-C, including whether it would cause harm if administered to humans.

claims.statement: In its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) briefing document evaluating MOTS-c (free base) and MOTS-c acetate for the 503A Bulks List, FDA staff state they did not identify any clinical studies or human exposure data for MOTS-c via any route of administration, and that both forms are not well-characterized from a physical/chemical characterization standpoint due to unavailable data on impurities, aggregates, and endotoxins; FDA staff recommended against adding either form to the list. At the PCAC meeting on July 23, 2026, the committee voted 7-5 with 2 abstentions to recommend MOTS-c for the 503A Bulks List, overriding the staff recommendation. An advisory committee vote is not itself a legal listing decision -- FDA must still complete rulemaking before MOTS-c could be lawfully compounded under 503A -- and the staff's underlying findings on the absence of human exposure data and incomplete characterization remain unchanged by the vote.

claims.statement: No published controlled human study of exogenously administered MOTS-c establishing efficacy for metabolic, fat-loss, exercise-performance, or anti-aging outcomes was identified; the only human MOTS-c data located is observational measurement of endogenous (naturally produced) circulating MOTS-c rising during exercise, and FDA's own review found no clinical studies or human exposure data for administered MOTS-c. conflicts.summary: A gray-market vendor page (gethealthspan.com) asserted a human RCT found a 15% improvement in insulin-stimulated glucose disposal from a single 2 mg/kg IV dose of MOTS-c, citing 'Reynolds, Bhatt, Patel et al. (2021) Nature Communications 12(1), 470' -- while FDA's PCAC briefing document states it did not identify any clinical studies or human exposure data for MOTS-c via any route of administration. RESOLVED 2026-08-29: direct fetch of the vendor page confirms the exact fabricated citation text, and direct fetch of the actual Reynolds et al. 2021 Nature Communications paper (DOI 10.1038/s41467-020-20790-0) shows a completely different author byline (Reynolds, Lai, Woodhead, Joly, Mitchell, Cameron-Smith, Lu, Cohen, Graham, Benayoun, Merry, Lee -- no Bhatt or Patel) and no IV-dose human RCT or glucose-clamp study of any kind; its only human data is an observational measurement of endogenous MOTS-c during exercise. An independent 2024 systematic review (Diabetology & Metabolic Syndrome, DOI 10.1186/s13098-024-01405-w) separately confirms zero controlled human trials of administered/exogenous MOTS-c exist in the literature. The vendor's cited human RCT does not exist as described; the citation is fabricated/misattributed, not merely unverifiable.
